1:
The praise of wisdom is read as a face. Keil and Delitzsch say that wisdom draws the veil from the countenance and makes it clear, and that what is meant is not merely brightening but the transfiguration by which, even in a face not beautiful, we discover the educated man above the common rank; they reject a rendering that doubles the brightness as untenable. John Wesley puts it in a sentence, that the face is put for the mind because the mind discovers itself in the countenance, and glosses the changed boldness as roughness turned to gentleness. Adam Clarke agrees that every state of the heart shines through the countenance, there being such evidence of a contented and benevolent soul in the face of a truly pious man that it cannot be mistaken. Matthew Henry compares the shining to the lawgiver’s coming down from the mount, and takes the knowledge of the interpretation for understanding the times and their critical junctures. Charles Ellicott and Clarke both report that the word for interpretation occurs elsewhere only in the Chaldee parts of one prophet, and Clarke that in the Hebrew the first clause closes the preceding chapter.

At the counsel about the king’s commandment Ellicott finds a defect in the text and a hint about the author. The verse begins with an unconnected pronoun, which he takes to show that a word dropped early out of the text, though the book is marked by a superfluous use of that pronoun; and he observes that counsels of this kind are not what one would expect from Solomon but from a man who had lived under a despotism. On the oath of God he rejects the historic references proposed, calling it idle to cite a historian’s report of a ruler exacting an oath from Jewish subjects, since this book has no connection with Egypt and the Bible itself supplies the usage. Clarke reads the clause as a courtier’s rule, that he keeps the mouth of the king and meddles not with state secrets, and reports that the Jewish princes swore fidelity to their kings. John Gill qualifies the obedience, which holds when the command agrees with the law of God.

The warning against going out of his sight turns two of them into political writers. Clarke takes the first five verses as directions to courtiers, quotes the Latin motto of the despot — I will this, I command that, my will is law — and observes that such governments see many revolutions, though without amendment, one tyrant rising to destroy another and then ruling as his predecessor did; he ends by preferring, after long trial, the mixed monarchy of his own country. Ellicott stays with the grammar and reaches the same subject: he refuses the claim that going out of the king’s sight means withdrawing allegiance, which would make the evil thing a conspiracy, since a counsel not to be hasty in rebelling rather than not to rebel is inconsistent with the context.

Keil and Delitzsch keep the duty in view, that the service due to the king is not to be thoughtlessly avoided, citing a rabbinic saying that the wise man is not hasty in answering. At the fourth verse they note that what is said here of the king is elsewhere said of God, and belongs especially to a despotic monarch, and they set the passage beside two apostolic sentences on obedience to authority. Ellicott adds that the word for power also occurs again only in that prophet, and that the second half of the verse is one of many reminiscences of the book of Job. Gill and Wesley take the verses upward: Gill reads the sight one cannot flee as the presence of the King of kings and the word that carries power as the word of the Gospel; Wesley grounds the obedience in the oath to keep all God’s laws.
5:
Whose commandment is meant is settled by the context. Keil and Delitzsch hold that it is not God’s but the king’s, and generally any appointment of the superior authority, since the passage treats not of God but of the ruler of a state; they reject a rendering by which the keeper of the commandment engages with no evil thing, because the verb is never so used, and take it in its sense of coming to know, by suffering and then by experience. John Gill allows both, an earthly king’s command when it agrees with the laws, or the heavenly King’s. John Wesley marks a new subject here. Adam Clarke takes the time and judgment practically: it is a great matter to discern when and how to speak and act, and when those are settled the question remains what to speak and do; to discern all this and act suitably is a lesson for a philosopher and a study for a Christian.

The sixth verse defeats two of them, and both say so. Charles Ellicott writes that the connecting particles present difficulties which have not been satisfactorily solved, and that words have even been conjectured to have dropped out of the text; the first half repeats an earlier verse and the second almost verbally another, and on that ground he prefers the rendering misery to wickedness. Keil and Delitzsch lay the same complaint on the author, that by repeating one particle through four clauses he renders exposition difficult, leaving free space for taking each as confirming or as hypothetical; their own construction makes one clause parenthetical and the next a supposition, that the wise man comes to experience an end and a decision if guilt has reached its full measure. Clarke keeps the verse severe: the word means every volition, and since a man generally has opportunity to do what he purposes, and his purposes are frequently evil, his acts are so too.

Matthew Henry answers the same verse with providence. All events concerning us, he says, with the exact time of them, are determined in the counsel of God and determined in wisdom, the time appointed in righteousness as well, so that the appointment is chargeable with neither folly nor iniquity; but we are much in the dark about what is to come, since a man does not know what shall be himself and no one can tell him when or how; therefore it is our wisdom to expect and prepare for sudden changes. Gill and Wesley put the ignorance more narrowly, Gill that a man does not know whether he shall have again the opportunity he has lost, Wesley that men are ignorant of future events and their minds therefore disquieted.

The four denials of the eighth verse are variously read. Keil and Delitzsch read them against the man who heaps up sins and carries his guilt until it overwhelms him unforeseen; their instance is the tyrant, who does not know that he will die by assassination and whom no one can tell how it will happen, so that he might arrange for his protection. Gill refuses to read the first clause of the wind, asking to what purpose that would be mentioned, and offers two readings: a check upon arbitrary princes, who have no power over the spirits or consciences of men, whatever power they hold over bodies and estates; or an argument for subjects, who cannot restrain the wrath of princes. Clarke reports three ways of taking the verse: a paraphrase in which no man can rule the breath so as to keep the life in the body; plain maxims about the wind, the day of death and the soldier who cannot be discharged till the war ends; and a reading that applies the whole to the tyrant, who must account to God, who shall die and cannot prevent it, and whose wickedness will not deliver him.
9:
Whose hurt is meant when one man rules over another is not agreed. Charles Ellicott states the ambiguity: the word own might be dropped, and the verse understood of the misery a tyrant inflicts on his subject, but the context speaks rather of how little the oppressor gains by his oppression. Matthew Henry reports that many take it of the hurt of the ruled, and presses the point: rulers who ought to be ministers for good use their power to invade property and encroach on liberty, and it is sad with a people when those who should protect their religion and rights aim at the destruction of both. Adam Clarke says that such men, instead of feeding, fleece the flock, and adds his own geography, that all this relates to the despots of the East and has always been more applicable to them than to any other sovereigns. John Wesley takes the hurt to fall on the ruler, who by tyranny brings the vengeance of God on his own head.

The tenth verse is the crux of the chapter, and each renders it differently. Keil and Delitzsch translate that the wicked were buried and came to rest, while those who acted justly had to depart from the holy place and were forgotten in the city, and see two classes of men in view. Ellicott explains where the ambiguity lies, since the word rendered so is elsewhere rendered well; on that reading the wicked receive an honourable burial while those who acted well are driven from the holy place and forgotten, but he prefers to render it the same way twice, so that the oppressor’s prosperity is temporary, death and forgetfulness coming soon. Clarke takes the holy place for the sacred office these men held, anointed as kings or priests, so that not having fulfilled it holily they are carried to their graves without lamentation and lie among the dead without remembrance. Wesley makes the throne itself the holy place, so called to aggravate the wickedness of men advanced to so sacred a trust, and finds the vanity in a glory so soon extinct. John Gill keeps to the pomp of the funeral, given to men who deserved no burial at all.

At the delayed sentence two of them stop on the word and disagree about it. Clarke calls it a Chaldee word, found only in the later books and nowhere else in this one; Ellicott calls it a Persian word, found in the same three books. Both draw the same moral from the delay, Clarke that because God does not immediately punish every delinquency men think he disregards evil acts, so that the longsuffering which leads to repentance is abused into an occasion of further crimes; Ellicott and Wesley more briefly, that forbearance makes men presumptuous. Gill turns the delay to account on the other side, as the patience God exercises toward his own people as well as toward the wicked, and as a display of his perfections.

The two verses that follow are the answer to that presumption, and they turn on a particle. Keil and Delitzsch refuse the rendering adopted by several, that though a sinner do evil a hundred times and live long, yet I know it shall be well with them that fear God; the particle that opens the clause cannot mean although, they say, but only considering that. Gill notes that one version reads a hundred years for a hundred times, and states what the two verses are for: to check the boldness of the sinner who presumes on the patience of God, and to make the people of God easy under the delay of justice and the prosperity of the wicked. Henry had drawn the same conclusion from the ruler he complained of, that the abuse of power is not the last word upon it.
14:
The vanity of the fourteenth verse is the old perplexity, and Matthew Henry names it: how the prosperity of the wicked and the troubles of the righteous can be reconciled with the holiness and goodness of the God who governs the world. His counsel is first not to be surprised, as at some strange thing, since the writer saw it in his own day: just men to whom it happened according to the work of the wicked, suffering as if punished for some great crime, and wicked men to whom it happened according to the work of the righteous, prospering as if rewarded for some good deed; so that the just are perplexed in their own minds while the wicked are easy and secure. John Wesley divides the cause two ways, either wicked potentates, who advance unworthy men and oppress those of most merit, or the providence of God, who sees it fit for weighty reasons so to manage this world. John Gill is careful that the vanity is not on God’s part, who has wise ends in it, for the trial of his people or the hardening of sinners. Charles Ellicott notes that the word rendered happeneth is used in this sense in only one other place, and Adam Clarke refers back to an earlier chapter.

At the commendation of mirth Clarke does what none of the others do: he assigns the verse to a speaker. These are more of the cavils of the infidel objector, he says, whose argument runs that since virtue is often oppressed and vice triumphs we should not trouble ourselves about things to come; and he gives the objector’s motto, eat, drink and play, for after death there is no pleasure. Wesley comes near the same reading in five words, that the merriment here is sensual delight. Keil and Delitzsch treat the verse as the author’s own conclusion, met with in similar form three times earlier, and dispute only whether the clause about what accompanies a man is jussive or subjunctive, against several who take it as indicative. Ellicott also marks it as a return to a sentiment already expressed, and notes that its three words stand together in an earlier book. Gill makes the mirth innocent, a cheerfulness in whatever condition, better than fretting at the prosperity of the wicked.

The closing verses Clarke reads as the reply to that objector, the rest as the writer’s own confession of ignorance. Clarke sets out the answer: God governs the world, but we cannot see the reasons of his conduct; we may study night and day and never fathom the depths of the divine government, though all is right and just; this life is a probation in which neither can the wicked be punished nor the righteous rewarded, but eternity is at hand, and the man who spends his life in eating and drinking will find in that day that he has lost the time in which he might have prepared for it. At the last verse he counts three refusals, that a man cannot find it out, that labouring will not help him, and that the most instructed of men shall not be able either; from which he turns on the objector, whose cavils about providence are vain because he cannot comprehend what he criticises. Keil and Delitzsch remark on the shape of the sentence rather than its sense, that a long period has formed itself under the author’s hand without a premeditated plan, halved by the conjunction in the middle. Gill is careful that the work of God meant is not creation but providence, whose steps he had viewed to find some general rule and found none. Wesley draws the practical end, that since no man however wise can perfectly understand these things, it is best not to perplex oneself with endless enquiries but to submit and live in the fear of God.
